lead: A perpetual motion machine of the first kind, PMM-1, is a claimed device that makes energy. It either gives net work in a complete cycle with no heat input, or gives more work than the heat it receives, so its efficiency is above 100 percent. The first law of thermodynamics forbids both forms because energy is conserved. Inventors still propose such machines, and engineers screen them with a cycle energy balance. Most syllabi treat PMM-1 as a named topic, usually beside the first-law statement. The idea is used to reject impossible energy claims before money is spent.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.1 for the cycle form ∮δQ = ∮δW.

sections.h3: The two claims and the cycle balance

blocks.text: For a closed system, Q is heat added to the system and W is work done by the system, both in kJ. The symbol ∮ means sum over a complete cycle. The small amounts δQ and δW are heat and work for one part of the cycle. Chapter 2.1 gives the cycle balance:

blocks.where: Q is heat added to the system in kJ; W is work done by the system in kJ; ∮ sums over the complete cycle.

blocks.text: A PMM-1 has two equivalent forms. Form 1: a machine completes a cycle, exchanges no heat, and still gives net work. Form 2: a heat engine in a cycle gives more net work W<sub>net</sub> than the heat Q<sub>in</sub> supplied to it, so its thermal efficiency η = W<sub>net</sub>/Q<sub>in</sub> is greater than 1, above 100 percent. Here Q<sub>in</sub> is heat supplied to the engine in kJ, and W<sub>net</sub> is net work out in the cycle in kJ. Set Q<sub>net</sub> = 0 in the cycle balance. The result is W<sub>net</sub> = 0. A no-heat cycle cannot deliver work. If a claim gives W<sub>net</sub> > Q<sub>net</sub>, then Q<sub>net</sub> − W<sub>net</sub> < 0. Energy would be created, so the first law rejects the claim.

Thermal efficiency is η = W<sub>net</sub>/Q<sub>in</sub>. Here W<sub>net</sub> is net work out in the cycle, in kJ, and Q<sub>in</sub> is heat supplied to the engine, in kJ. For a cycle, W<sub>net</sub> = Q<sub>net</sub> = Q<sub>in</sub> − Q<sub>out</sub>, where Q<sub>out</sub> is heat rejected. For a real engine Q<sub>out</sub> ≥ 0, so W<sub>net</sub> ≤ Q<sub>in</sub> and η ≤ 1, that is ≤ 100 percent. A claim of 125 percent means that for every 100 kJ of heat supplied, 125 kJ of work comes out; the extra 25 kJ, 25 percent of the heat input, was never converted from heat.

Exam wording often gives input and output in kW for a closed-cycle claim. Compute Q<sub>in</sub>, Q<sub>out</sub> and W. Check that W = Q<sub>in</sub> − Q<sub>out</sub>. If W is more than Q<sub>in</sub>, energy is being created and the claim is a PMM-1. If W is less than Q<sub>in</sub>, the difference is simply heat rejected, which is allowed. Do not reject it by saying 'efficiency is too low'; that is not the first-law test.
PMM-2 is different. It obeys the first law; it does not create energy. It breaks the second law by converting a single heat reservoir fully into work. First-law tests cannot reject PMM-2; see Unit 3.

figure.caption: The machine claims work from no heat input. The cycle balance Q_net = W_net then forces W_net = 0, so the claim fails.

spec.title: Why PMM-1 fails
spec.aria: A machine with no heat input claims a work output, and the cycle energy balance rejects that claim.

examples.question: An inventor claims a closed-cycle machine takes in 300 kW of heat and delivers 500 kW of shaft work, with no other energy exchange. A second claim takes in 200 kW of heat and delivers 250 kW of work. Test both claims.
steps: First claim: Q_net = 300 kW and W_net = 500 kW.
Cycle balance requires W_net = Q_net. The excess is 500 − 300 = 200 kW.
That 200 kW would be created energy. The claim violates the first law, so it is a PMM-1.
In percent, η = 1.25 × 100 = 125 percent. Efficiency above 100 percent is impossible, so this claim is also PMM-1.
examples.answer: Both claims are impossible: the first creates 200 kW, and the second claims 125 percent efficiency.
examples.check:
q1_in = 300.0
w1_out = 500.0
excess = w1_out - q1_in
q2_in = 200.0
w2_out = 250.0
eta = w2_out / q2_in
eta_pct = eta * 100.0
print(excess)
print(eta)
print(eta_pct)

traps: Using Q_in in place of Q_net in a cycle; the cycle balance uses net heat.
Calling a low-efficiency device a PMM-1; low efficiency is inefficiency, not energy creation.
Confusing PMM-1 with PMM-2; PMM-2 obeys the first law and fails the second.
Mixing kW and kJ in a cycle claim; kW is a rate, kJ is an amount, so use one basis.
Sign convention slip: heat added is positive, work done by the system is positive.

quiz.a: A device that in a cycle gives net work with no heat input, or gives more work than heat input (η > 100 percent).

quiz.q: Why does ∮δQ = ∮δW forbid a no-heat work-producing cycle?
quiz.a: With Q_net = 0, the balance gives W_net = 0, so no net work can be delivered.

quiz.q: A cycle takes 80 kW heat, rejects 20 kW, and gives 60 kW work. Is it PMM-1?
quiz.a: Q_net = 80 − 20 = 60 kW = W_net. The balance holds, so it is not PMM-1.

quiz.q: A claim has Q_in = 400 kW and η = 110 percent. Find W_net and decide.
quiz.a: W_net = 1.10 × 400 = 440 kW. It exceeds Q_in by 40 kW, creating energy, so it is PMM-1.

quiz.q: Give one line that separates PMM-1 from PMM-2.
quiz.a: PMM-1 breaks the first law; PMM-2 obeys the first law but breaks the second law.

quiz.q: In a complete cycle Q_net = 0. What is W_net?

beyond: Not for the exam. Patent offices see perpetual-motion claims, and examiners use energy balances to reject them. Industry uses the same check in energy audits, where measured heat and work must close to within instrument error. Simulation software flags a component when its energy balance does not close. Search for 'first law energy balance check' and 'patent perpetual motion rejection' to see how the rule is applied.
